studentRecords.vocab:
We got to learn the difference between mostly used professional terms that could be easily mixed up each others.

The difference between LANDSIDE and AIRSIDE. The landside is the first area we got to walk in while entering an airport. It is accessible to anyone. The airside is the secured operational area beyond the security checkpoint. It includes all the different areas of the airport that are beyond the security gate. 

the difference between AIRLINE and AERODROME OPERATOR. The airline owns the aircrafts and provide commercial passenger and cargo air transports. The aerodrome operator owns the airport infrastructure in itself and enable airlines to provide flights services to their customers.

The difference between SCHEDULED FLIGHT and CHARTER FLIGHT. A scheduled flight is fixed and provided regardless of passenger load while a charter flight is one flight booked by a specific organization for a specific slot of time.

The distinction between a DELAY and a FLIGHT CANCELLATION. A delay means that the flight will still be provided but within a different slot time from the originally scheduled one. A flight cancellation means that the flight has been called off. In this situation the passengers will either be allocated to alternative flights or fully refund with statutory compensations.

We also got to learn some abbreviations. 
AODB for Airport Operational DataBase (that manages flight schedules, stand allocations and gate changes)
TRC for Turnaround Coordinator (the airside manager who supervises all ground activities between arrival and departure)
GPU for Ground Power Unit (a mobile generator that provides electricity and air conditioning to the aircraft with engines and APU off)
GSE for Ground Support Equipment (all mobile ground equipment that ensure ground manoeuvre)

studentRecords.vocab:
We started this session with some vocabulary synonyms depending on the country we find ourselves into. We particularly enlightened the APRON used in GB that is called the RAMP in the USA. This led us to mention the difference in both countries accent. The British accent is described as NON RHOTIC while the USA accent is RHOTIC. 

Then we worked on some vocabulary from the previous session in pair. We had to explain our working partner what we had understand of these words. We especially treated the following ones : UNRULLY PASSENGERS, ANCILLARY REVENUE, PASSENGER RIGHTS and TURNAROUND TIME.
studentRecords.content:
All along the session we had opportunities to discuss new professional vocabulary with our teacher such as HANDWAND that is a sort of mobile device used to detect any metallic things such as blade that people can carry around. A RIP OFF that is an act of theft by a conman. To FILL UP a tank with oil or SAF (Sustainable Aviation Fuel). A MANUFACTURER is a plane builder such as Embraer in Brazil. TO BE PROBLEMATIC (and not a problematic) is similar to an issue or a challenge. The CONCOURSE is a large haul inside the airport where people can move around (it is not to be confused with the BOTTLE NECK that is a narrow corridor passengers walk through to board a plane. 

The distance of a flight will makes us describe it as SHORT, MEDIUM or LONG HAUL. 

finally we could make a differentiation between a CONVEYER BELT and a CAROUSEL and also between SAFETY (describe protection from unintentional harm) and SECURITY (describe protection against intentional harm).

We could discuss some new vocabulary in pair working. LANDSIDE CHECK IN and BAG DROP are both part of a procedure when people can print themselves their boarding pass and baggage tags inside the airport and then deposit their luggage at an automated conveyer. 

SECURITY SCREENING CHECKPOINT is when luggage go through X-rays while passengers walk through metal detectors or body scanners. 

AIRSIDE CONCOURSE is an inner area in the airside where people can walk along while intending to board an airplane. 

DWELL TIME is a time people wait between arriving from a flight and departing for the next one. 

The BOARDING GATE is a check in point that people must go through before boarding a plane walking across the JET BRIDGE. 

SPECIAL ASSISTANCE consist on a ground team that helps disabled passenger to board a plane using technical tools such as specialized lifts or protocol like priority boarding.

studentRecords.vocab:
- seek assistance : look for assistance when you have a problem with an automatic machine at an airport
- to get upgraded : in aviation, to get a business class ticket while you bought an economy class one
- to overbook a flight : when airlines sell more tickets than available seats in a plane, sometimes leading to denied boarding
- to extend a stay : to decide to stay longer than expected somewhere because you really like the place for example
- in the driver's seat : to be in charge or in control of a situation 
- off the beaten track : when you choose a place where few people go, sometimes far from towns and roads 
- to miss a connection : when you have to switch to another plane to go somewhere, this is a connection. But if the first plane is late, you can miss this connection.
- to hit the road : to leave a place, to start a journey
- a direct flight : a flight which operates under the same flight number but can do some stops, unlike a non-stop flight 
- to clear customs : when you officially go through a country's border with the permission of the customs authority 
- a round trip : when you buy tickets to flight to a destination and return to your starting point (with a return ticket), unlike a single ticket
- an itinerary : it is a planned route for a journey or trip, it is the path you follow
- a boarding pass : travel document essential to go through the boarding gate 
- carbon footprint : amount of greenhouse gases released in the atmosphere. It's different depending on the transport you use
- all-inclusive : when the price of your ticket covers every accommodation in the plane such as meals, drinks...
The words we learned today are mainly used in aviation and vacation contexts.

studentRecords.vocab:
We learnt a lot of vocabulary today :
- push-back tug : the vehicle which push the aircraft outside the parking stand. It's also known as a tug.
- jet bridge : a telescopic bridge linking the airport (the boarding gate) to the aircraft (the airplane door). It's mainly used for big airplanes while we use moving stairs for the others.
- apron/ramp : the parking area where the aircraft wait during the turnaround time. It's located in the airside.
- windsock : fabric tube which shows both the direction and the speed of the wind. This is essential for any aerodrome in the world.
- duty free : buying something without paying local or national import duties. This is common in the international transit areas such as airports.
- dwell time : the time passengers spend in the terminal (security and boarding check-in...). New technologies like bio-metric e-gate, facial recognition and automated bag drop are useful to reduce this time.
- automated bag drop : a way to register and drop your luggage by yourself  
- runway-holding position : a specific place (a big line on the floor) where the aircraft has to stop and wait for instructions. This is like a border between the taxiway and the runway.
- baggage conveyor belt : moving track which transports checked luggage automatically between different points in the airport. It's also known as a baggage carousel.
studentRecords.content:
We talked about some new technologies like the bio-metric e-gates, automated bag drop and facial recognition because this is more and more used in the airports to reduce the dwell time. We saw that these solutions are interesting but there are some concerns about it. For example, a lot of people wonder if their personal data are really deleted after a check-in with a bio-metric or facial recognition gate. We also highlighted the impact of these new solutions on the world of work. In fact, it could lead to the disappearance of some jobs. 
Finally, we learnt how to use prepositions of place, direction and movement depending on the situation.
studentRecords.needs: Today's session was great to learn new vocabulary but I still need to improve my fluency and my pronunciation for some words (I can't say words like throughout, bought etc).
studentRecords.helpFe: Today's session brought us a lot of vocabulary which is a great thing. It helps us to understand better the airport environment and it allows us to speak about really specific topics in aviation without always looking for a specific word.

topBuzzwords.definition: Landside = public areas before security (check-in, arrivals hall). Airside = strictly secured operations areas beyond security (gates, apron, taxiways, runways).
The designated paved area where aircraft park at designated stands to board/deboard, refuel, load baggage, and undergo ground servicing.
Essential communicative collocations: to book a flight, to board a plane, to check in, to clear customs, and to travel with carry-on luggage.
GPU (Ground Power Unit) = mobile ground generator supplying electricity at the gate. APU (Auxiliary Power Unit) = small gas turbine in the aircraft tail used when engines and GPU are off.

topBuzzwords.term: Travel Idioms (Scenic Route, Hit the Road)
topBuzzwords.definition: Conversational storytelling idioms: to hit the road (depart), to take the scenic route (longer picturesque path), and to be in the driver's seat (in control).
TRC = Turnaround Coordinator supervising ramp tasks between flight arrival and departure. AODB = Airport Operational Database managing flight schedules, gate changes, and allocated stands.
A traveler who refuses to follow crew instructions or behaves disruptively, risking flight diversions, police arrest, and heavy airline costs.
LCC = budget airline offering cheap baseline tickets. Ancillary Revenue = extra income from non-ticket sales (carry-on bags, seat selection, on-board meals).
Scheduled = timetabled regular airline service. Charter = booked on-demand for a specific private/tour group. Severe delays trigger passenger statutory care.

topBuzzwords.term: Get Off to a Flying Start & Word of Mouth
topBuzzwords.definition: Get off to a flying start = beginning a semester or project with immediate success and momentum. Word of mouth = organic communication from person to person.
When an airline sells more tickets than available seats in anticipation of no-shows, risking involuntary denied boarding and statutory compensation obligations.
Direct flight = keeps the same single flight number but may include intermediate tech stops. Non-stop flight = flies between origin and destination with zero stops.

grammarTrapsCaught.title: ❌ 'Luggages' and 'Trainings' do NOT exist!
grammarTrapsCaught.rule: Both 'luggage' and 'training' are uncountable nouns in English. Never add an 's'.
grammarTrapsCaught.correctExample: ✅ "We checked three pieces of luggage and completed our training course."

grammarTrapsCaught.title: 🗣️ Pronunciation Trap: Itinerary
grammarTrapsCaught.rule: Multiple students flagged pronunciation difficulty with 'itinerary'. Stress is on the second syllable: /aɪˈtɪn.ər.ər.i/ (eye-TIN-er-uh-ree).
grammarTrapsCaught.correctExample: ✅ "Could you please confirm our flight itinerary before we head to the gate?"

grammarTrapsCaught.title: ⏱️ Reported Speech Backshift & Time References
grammarTrapsCaught.rule: When reporting past dialogue, tenses shift back (present -> past, past -> past perfect; will -> would), and time adverbs shift ('today' -> 'that day', 'yesterday' -> 'the day before', 'tomorrow' -> 'the following day').
grammarTrapsCaught.correctExample: ✅ "He said he was running on empty that day and would take the train the following morning."

grammarTrapsCaught.title: 📍 Preposition Trap: At vs. In vs. Into
grammarTrapsCaught.rule: Watch out for spatial prepositions: use 'at' for a specific point/facility (at the airport, at the gate), 'in' for an enclosed space (in the cabin), and 'into' for direction/movement (boarded into the aircraft).
grammarTrapsCaught.correctExample: ✅ "We arrived at Toulouse-Blagnac Airport, waited at gate 12, and boarded into the aircraft."

grammarTrapsCaught.title: ✈️ Apron vs. Taxiway vs. Runway
grammarTrapsCaught.rule: Exact spatial precision is required in operational briefings. Never refer to the runway when you mean parking on the apron or taxiing on taxiway Alpha.
grammarTrapsCaught.correctExample: ✅ "The aircraft pushed back from stand B4 onto the apron, taxied via Charlie, and lined up on Runway 14L."

grammarTrapsCaught.title: 💡 'Used to do' vs. 'Be used to doing'
grammarTrapsCaught.rule: 'I used to work' expresses a past habit that is finished. 'I am used to working' means you are accustomed/familiar with it now.
grammarTrapsCaught.correctExample: ✅ "I used to live in Paris, but now I am used to living in Toulouse."
